subject: orthopaedics
title: Osteomyelitis: sequestra, sinuses and dead-space surgery

steps.tx: Acute **haematogenous osteomyelitis** affects children when bacteria lodge in the slow loops of the **metaphysis** during bacteraemia. **Staphylococcus aureus** causes most cases, while Salmonella classically infects bone infarcts in sickle cell disease. The child has throbbing pain, fever and refusal to move the tender swollen limb. Blood cultures and aspiration come before antibiotics whenever the child stays stable enough.
steps.say: Bacteria reach growing bone through the bloodstream and settle near the growth plate. Sluggish blood flow in that region lets the organisms lodge and multiply quickly. The child develops fever and severe local pain and refuses to move the limb. Doctors collect blood and pus samples before starting antibiotic treatment whenever possible. Early treatment can protect the growth plate and the nearby joint from damage.

steps.tx: In chronic disease a **sequestrum** is dead detached bone, and the living **involucrum** forms a sheath of new bone around it. Holes called **cloacae** drain pus to a skin sinus that discharges for years, as this diagram shows. A Brodie abscess forms a small walled cavity, while Garre disease thickens bone without pus. Staging by anatomy and host health guides the surgical plan.
steps.say: The diagram will label the dead fragment that sits at the centre of chronic infection. New living bone wraps around that fragment and forms a protective outer sheath. Openings in the sheath let pus escape toward a discharging track on the skin. Naming each part correctly helps the surgeon plan complete removal of dead bone. Leaving dead bone behind allows the infection to flare again later.

vis.alt: Diagram showing chronic osteomyelitis with a central sequestrum, surrounding involucrum, cloacae, and a draining sinus tract to the skin.
vis.caption: Chronic osteomyelitis: sequestrum, involucrum, cloacae, sinus

steps.tx: **Vertebral osteomyelitis** infects the disc and endplates of adults and causes deep local back pain. A diabetic foot ulcer that probes to bone strongly suggests bone infection beneath the ulcer. **Biofilm** on a prosthesis causes indolent loosening that blood tests may barely reveal. Deep biopsy and culture confirm the organism before long treatment begins in doubtful cases.
steps.say: Infection can reach bone from the blood, from a nearby ulcer, or around an implant. Adult spinal infection destroys the disc space and the facing vertebral surfaces together. A foot ulcer that touches bone during gentle probing suggests deep infection below. Germs on an artificial joint hide inside a protective film and resist antibiotics. Deep samples taken at surgery identify the organism most reliably.

steps.tx: This sagittal scan shows a bright infected disc with **endplate oedema** in the lumbar spine and surrounding inflammation. The picture illustrates **vertebral osteomyelitis**, which the lesson lists among its special forms in adults. It matters because back pain with this scan pattern needs culture and prolonged antibiotics, not simple analgesia. For the exam, read the disc and both facing endplates together as one infected unit.
steps.say: The side view scan shows one disc glowing brightly between two vertebral bodies. Both facing surfaces of those bodies show swelling that signals active infection nearby. Soft tissue behind the spine also looks inflamed and thickened on the image. This combined pattern separates spinal infection from simple age related disc wear. Examiners expect you to name the disc and endplates as one involved unit.

vis.alt: Sagittal lumbar spine MRI showing hyperintense disc, endplate edema and paravertebral inflammation
vis.caption: Sagittal lumbar MRI showing infected disc and endplate edema. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Treatment starts with cultures before antibiotics, then covers **Staphylococcus aureus** and gram negative organisms as local policy directs. Therapy runs for **four to six weeks** in many cases, moving from intravenous to oral drugs. Surgery removes dead bone by **sequestrectomy**, saucerises the cavity and fills the dead space with muscle or graft. Falling inflammatory markers track progress, while follow up lasts for years.
steps.say: Good treatment begins with samples that identify the causative organism accurately. Antibiotics then target that organism for several weeks of sustained therapy. Surgery removes every piece of dead bone that shelters bacteria from drugs. Muscle flaps or bone graft fill the empty space left after cleaning. Blood markers fall as infection settles, but late relapse remains possible.
